## Handing Time Series in R

```{r}
sales <- read.csv("sales_data.csv")

# Run once — install anything missing
pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "tsibble", "feasts", "fable", "timetk",
          "modeltime", "kableExtra", "here")
```

## Handing Dates and Aggregation

```{r}
# Load and filter data
df <- read.csv("sales_data.csv")
df$date <- as.Date(df$date)
df <- subset(df, store_id == "S001")

# Aggregate by Month using format()
agg_month <- aggregate(sales ~ format(date, "%Y-%m"), data = df, FUN = sum)

# Aggregate by Week (%U for week of the year)
agg_week <- aggregate(sales ~ format(date, "%Y-%U"), data = df, FUN = mean)

head(agg_month)

sales_ts <- ts(agg_month$sales, start = c(2021, 1), frequency = 12)

frequency(sales_ts)
start(sales_ts)
end(sales_ts)
cycle(sales_ts)
time(sales_ts)
window(sales_ts, start = c(2022, 1), end = c(2022, 12))
stats::lag(sales_ts, k = 1)
diff(sales_ts)
diff(sales_ts, lag = 12)
is.ts(sales_ts)
is.na(sales_ts)
na.omit(sales_ts)
```

## Helper conversions

```{r}
t <- time(sales_ts)

# Extract Year and Month
years <- floor(t)
months <- round(12 * (t - years)) + 1

data.frame(Decimal = as.numeric(t), Year = years, Month = months)
```

## Subsetting with window

```{r}
# Extract only the second half of 2023
sub_ts <- window(sales_ts, start = c(2023, 7), end = c(2023, 12))
print(sub_ts)
```

## Lags and differences

```{r}
# Shift the time index forward by 1 period (does not move the values)
lagged_ts <- stats::lag(sales_ts, k = -1)

# First-order differencing (removes linear trend)
diff_ts <- diff(sales_ts, differences = 1)

# Seasonal differencing (removes a 12-month seasonal pattern)
seasonal_diff_ts <- diff(sales_ts, lag = 12)

diff_ts
```

## Combining Series: `ts.union()` and `ts.intersect()`

```{r}
ts_a <- ts(1:10, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)
ts_b <- ts(11:18, start = c(2023, 4), frequency = 12)

# Union: keeps full range, fills gaps with NA
combined_union <- ts.union(ts_a, ts_b)

# Intersect: keeps only the overlapping months
combined_intersect <- ts.intersect(ts_a, ts_b)

combined_intersect
```

## Checking for missing values

```{r}
has_na <- anyNA(sales_ts)
cat("Contains missing values:", has_na, "\n")
```

## Time series plots

```{r}
plot.ts(sales_ts,
        main = "Monthly Observations 2021-2024 for Store 1",
        xlab = "Year/Month",
        ylab = "Measurement Units",
        col = "darkred",
        lwd = 2,
        lty = 1,
        type = "o",
        pch = 16)

plot(sales_ts,
     main = "Simplified Time Plot",
     col = "blue",
     lty = 2)

# naive decomposition 
decomp <- decompose(sales_ts)
plot(decomp)
```

## **Modern Time Series Analysis: tidyverts, timetk, and modeltime**

```{r}
# Core packages used in this section
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr, ggplot2, readr, lubridate
library(tsibble)      # tidy time series class: index + key
library(feasts)        # Feature extraction And Statistics for Time Series
library(timetk)        # tidy plotting & diagnostics for ts/tibbles
#library(modeltime)      # unified tidymodels-style forecasting framework
```

## **Reading Data into a `tsibble`**

```{r}
library(readr)
library(tsibble)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Read raw data, forcing an explicit Date type on `date`
raw <- read_csv(
  "sales_data.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    date     = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    store_id = col_character(),
    sales    = col_double()
  )
)

# 2. Build the tsibble at its NATIVE granularity (daily) — one row per
#    (date, store_id) combination, so index and key are already unique
sales_tsbl <- raw %>%
  as_tsibble(index = date, key = store_id)

# 3. Check for implicit gaps in the time index (missing rows, not NA values)
has_gaps <- sales_tsbl %>% count_gaps()
print(has_gaps)

# 4. If gaps exist, fill them explicitly so operations don't silently misalign
sales_tsbl <- sales_tsbl %>% fill_gaps(.full = TRUE)

# 5. Only NOW aggregate to a coarser granularity, via index_by() + summarise()
sales_monthly <- sales_tsbl %>%
  index_by(month = ~ yearmonth(.)) %>%
  summarise(sales = sum(sales, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

## EDA with `feasts`

```{r}
library(feasts)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# Fill remaining NAs (per-store mean) before decomposition
sales_tsbl_filled <- sales_tsbl %>%
  group_by_key() %>%
  mutate(sales = tidyr::replace_na(sales, mean(sales, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  ungroup()

# Overall shape of the series (faceted automatically because of the key)
sales_tsbl_filled %>% autoplot(sales)
```

```{r}
# Compare seasonal cycles year over year (daily data has 2 plausible cycles —
# weekly and yearly — so `period` must be stated explicitly)
sales_tsbl_filled %>% gg_season(sales, period = "year", labels = "both")

sales_tsbl_filled %>% gg_season(sales, period = "week")

# Compare each calendar month's behaviour across years (the monthly aggregate
# is cleaner here than daily, since it removes the weekly cycle from view)
sales_monthly %>% gg_subseries(sales)

# Autocorrelation structure
sales_tsbl_filled %>% ACF(sales) %>% autoplot()

# STL decomposition (needs an explicit period on daily data too)
sales_tsbl_filled %>%
  model(STL(sales ~ trend() + season(period = "year"))) %>%
  components() %>%
  autoplot()


sales_tsbl_filled %>%
  features(sales, feat_stl)
```

## **Reading and Diagnosing Data with `timetk`**

```{r}
library(timetk)
library(readr)

# Read data — timetk works with a normal tibble; only a Date column is required
sales_tbl <- read_csv(
  "sales_data.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    date     = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    store_id = col_character(),
    sales    = col_double()
  )
)

# Interactive/static time series plot, grouped by store (no tsibble conversion needed)
sales_tbl %>%
  group_by(store_id) %>%
  plot_time_series(date, sales, .interactive = FALSE)

# Diagnose the time index: regularity, gaps, scale, timezone
sales_tbl %>% tk_summary_diagnostics(date)

# Seasonal decomposition / ACF diagnostics in one call
# Explicit .feature_set: daily data has no sub-day granularity, so
# "second"/"minute"/"hour" are meaningless here and are excluded.
sales_tbl %>%
  plot_seasonal_diagnostics(
    date, sales,
    .feature_set = c("wday.lbl", "week", "month.lbl", "quarter", "year"),
    .interactive = FALSE
  )

sales_tbl %>%
  plot_acf_diagnostics(date, sales, .interactive = FALSE)
```

## Plotting using all the different functions 

```{r}
library(timetk)

# Load and filter data
df <- read.csv("sales_data.csv")
df$date <- as.Date(df$date)
s1 <- subset(df, store_id == "S001")

# plot_time_series
s1 %>%
  plot_time_series(date, sales)

# tk_summary_diagnostics
s1 %>%
  tk_summary_diagnostics(date)

# plot_seasonal_diagnostics
s1 %>%
  plot_seasonal_diagnostics(date, sales)

# plot_acf_diagnostics
s1 %>%
  plot_acf_diagnostics(date, sales)

# plot_anomaly_diagnostics
s1 %>%
  plot_anomaly_diagnostics(date, sales)
```

## Question 7 - Answering code questions 

**Q1 — `ts(x, start = c(2023, 13), frequency = 12)`**\
This is invalid because monthly data only has 12 periods per year, so the second element of `start` can't exceed 12. Writing `c(2023, 13)` tries to say "period 13 of 2023," which doesn't exist — it should roll over to `c(2024, 1)` instead. Fix: `ts(x, start = c(2024, 1), frequency = 12)`.

**Q2 — `ts(x, start = 2023, frequency = 12)`**\
For sub-annual data (anything with `frequency > 1`), `start` needs to specify both the year *and* which period within that year you're starting at — a single number is ambiguous. Fix: `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)`.

**Q3 — `ts(x, start = c(2023, 0), frequency = 12)`**\
`ts()` uses 1-based indexing for periods, so period `0` doesn't exist within a year — the first month is period 1, not 0. Fix: `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)`.

**Q4 — `ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 4)`**\
The meaning of "period 2" depends entirely on what `frequency` you've set — with `frequency = 4` (quarterly), period 2 means Q2, not February. If the data is actually monthly, the frequency is wrong and needs to match the data's real periodicity. Fix: `ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 12)`.

**Q5 — `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12.5)`**\
`frequency` must be a whole number, since it represents a count of periods per cycle (you can't have half an observation per year). Many time-series methods that build on `ts` objects require an integer frequency to work at all. Fix: `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)`.

**Q6 — `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12, deltat = 1/12)`**\
`frequency` and `deltat` both describe the same thing (the spacing between observations) from two different angles — one as "how many per year," the other as "time between = 1/frequency" — so specifying both is redundant and R doesn't allow it. Fix: pick one; here, `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)`.

**Q7 — `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 365)`**\
`frequency = 365` tells R this is daily data, so if `x` is actually a vector of monthly values, the frequency doesn't match the actual data type/spacing — it would misassign what each value represents in the yearly cycle. Fix: `ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)`.

**Q8 — `window(x, start = c(2023, 13))`**\
`window()` can only extract a period that actually exists within the original series' time range — asking it to start at "month 13 of 2023" (or any point outside the series' bounds) has nothing to return. Fix: pick a start point inside the series, e.g. `window(x, start = c(2024, 1))`.

**Q9 — `decompose(ts(x, frequency = 1))`**\
`decompose()` splits a series into trend, seasonal, and random components — but with `frequency = 1`, there's no cycle at all (each "cycle" is a single point), so there's no seasonal pattern for it to extract, and it also needs at least two full cycles of data to estimate anything reliably. Fix: use a frequency that reflects real seasonality, e.g. `decompose(ts(x, frequency = 12))` for monthly data.
